rv.q: He’s also given himself a huge challenge. Nelson is a real pendejo—probably every day, but even more so today when they’re waiting for their son, Nick (Trey Santiago-Hudson, son of the play’s director, Ruben Santiago-Hudson), to return.
In recent years, Nelson’s ambition caused him to remove his family from their comfortable Latino-peopled environs of Jackson Heights to snooty Forest Hills, where the white neighbors are unwelcoming.

“I could have been a contender.” These words ran through my head as I watched John Leguizamo in his play The Other Americans at the Public Theater tear his way into the character of Nelson, the raging, multi-layered, vulnerable, family patriarch trying to get ahead, fighting a system where the ‘haves’ gate-keep their privilege, insuring certain...

An impressive collection of titles, to be sure, but one that is conspicuously missing Latino characters and cultures. Leguizamo the playwright seeks to fill that gap, even when the effort occasionally falls short. When The Other Americans begins, it’s not immediately apparent that those are the dramatic mountains Leguizamo is attempting to scale.

Nick’s sister (Rebecca Jiminez) wants nothing but the best for her little brother, short of having him follow her and her fiancé to Los Angeles to start independent lives. As an actor, Leguizamo harnesses his signature charm and social commentary, but as a playwright, The Other Americans drowns in its own exposition.

It’s a meaty, complicated role that Leguizamo has written for himself — and as an actor he persuasively demonstrates how a man who can often seem to be an absolute monster with a quick temper and obvious blind spots can also charm his way through life.
